method: Manual source-sufficiency review of paired public packets. No LLM judge and no frozen evaluator score.

constraints.lookup_rule: Each lookup is only a paraphrase or facet restatement derivable from the root question; no expected-answer-only vocabulary, guessed source names, or project identifiers.

rubric.sufficient: Visible public sources directly support a complete answer without guesswork or unsafe layer conflation.
rubric.partial: Visible sources support an important part but omit a requested distinction/condition or risk conflating different contract layers.
rubric.miss: Visible public sources do not support the requested answer.

cases.rationale: Lookup surfaces the public omitted-material contract; root returns unrelated MCP Packs.
Even with lookups the visible sources do not explain cut-short versus no-safe-evidence; comparison retrieval drifts to unrelated authority/library material.
Lookup surfaces the omitted-material contract stating truncation omits non-critical material.
Lookup directly surfaces the client-handling field list: status, kind, sources, missing, omitted_counts.
Both variants support using grounded visible sources without claiming completeness, but neither directly binds that guidance to truncation.
Lookup surfaces the no-safe-context meaning of insufficient evidence but not the full contrasting truncation semantics in the same visible packet.
Both variants return no usable source for the question whether omitted material makes an otherwise useful packet unusable.
Both expose omission/missing concepts, but the omission witness is the nested authoring-handoff contract rather than the normal public-response omission field, so layer distinction remains unsafe.
Lookup finds truncation semantics but not the recovery policy needed to answer whether increasing budget should be the first reaction.
Lookup directly surfaces the public client-handling fields.
Both surface the maintained-current-docs versus release-history authority rule.
Lookup changes the result from unrelated workflow guidance to the direct release-history authority rule.
Both directly support current maintained documentation as primary for present behavior.
Both directly support release history as primary for migration/history questions.
Both directly support maintained current documentation for current configuration.
API wording hijacks both variants toward API keys/registry material; the current-versus-history rule is not surfaced.
Lookup surfaces the direct rule that release/change history is a release-notes/CHANGELOG question.
Both surface the current source-of-truth rule; lookup also surfaces the present-state caveat.
Both directly state that historical notes may supplement but must not outrank current source-of-truth merely due feature-name overlap.
Root returns only a historical changelog example; lookup surfaces the authority rule needed to combine history with current documentation.
Both interpret split mainly as chunk splitting/indexing instead of retrieval-planning split semantics.
Lookup avoids total failure but still does not surface the same-need/different-vocabulary workflow rule.
Lookup surfaces the exact gap-directed rule: split only after the first packet leaves an independently answerable requested part missing.
Lookup surfaces the exact known-source rule: use the issued bounded source read instead of broad search.
Both surface the explicit stop rule: sufficient visible packet or no progress; unverified quality alone is not a reason to continue.
Lookup turns no evidence into the exact unverified-quality stopping rule.
Neither surfaces the documented at-most-one non-automatic rephrase rule.
Both surface typed next-action workflow guidance sufficiently to answer follow-the-returned-action rather than invent recovery.
Both surface targeted gap recovery within existing limits, sufficient to reject global budget/result-count inflation as the normal strategy.
Lookup surfaces the exact rule to target the concrete missing side/part after the first packet.

observations: Project-blind lookups materially improve final visible evidence, not merely metadata: strict sufficient cases rise from 9/30 to 20/30.
13/30 pairs improve by at least one rubric level; no pair worsens under the manual source-sufficiency rubric.
The remaining lookup-resistant failures are G02, G07, G09, G16, G21, G22, and G27.
Persistent failures cluster around semantic sense ambiguity, high-frequency distractor vocabulary, negation/stopping policy, and cross-section policy joins.
query_coverage/context_quality remain unsuitable as semantic answer scores; manual judgment is based on the visible sources.
